title: Abraham and Melchizedek as Types of Christ's Perfection
english: To bring us to completion in holiness, I say that the righteousness that is in Christ and the worship we offer through him are superior, as God himself has cried out through the voices of the prophets, who speak to those who have honored the lawful worship and have been loosed from the old commandment, saying at one time, 'Wash yourselves, become clean,' and at another time, 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than whole burnt offerings' (Isaiah 1:16, Hosea 6:6).
Through Christ, we have been shown mercy, and in him, we have seen the Father with our minds, and we have come to know the God who is by nature.

Eusebius, being exceedingly good, accumulates many things in addition to what has already been said, and he would also add the voices of the holy prophets, which make it clear that the worship according to the law is acceptable to God, but to avoid drawing out the discussion and going off on a tangent, we will now focus on the divinely spoken Abraham.

Abraham, having inquired about his nephew Lot, who had unexpectedly fallen into danger, armed his household and certain confederates, Eschol, Anan, and Mamre, and led them out against the victors, freeing Lot from their plunder, and with him, he rescued a great multitude that had gathered together and was still in danger.

As Abraham returned home, carrying the splendid manliness he had won against his enemies, those who had been helped through his labors were compelled to come and meet him, and it is written that the king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings with him, to the valley of Shaveh, which was the king's plain.

Then Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine to Abraham, and as the priest of God Most High, he blessed Abraham, saying, 'Blessed be Abraham by God Most High, who made heaven and earth, and blessed be God Most High, who delivered your enemies into your hand', and Abraham gave him tithes from all (Genesis 14:18-20).

Considering the types in Christ's perfection that are clearly reflected in Melchizedek, and the measure of the legal worship that is diminished, it is evident that the lesser is blessed by the better, as is written, and Abraham, the root of those from Israel, and Levi, who was adorned with the ornaments of the divine priesthood and who excelled and was extraordinary, was yet lying in the loins of his father when he met with him.
translator_notes: Greek ends mid-word/mid-sentence: 'ὅτε συνήντησεν α' (when he met [with]...). The literal rendering of the edge fragment is retained.
The number '69.84' appears to be OCR corruption or non-textual and has been omitted.
Name forms: Eschol, Anan, and Mamre are preserved as per source spelling.

title: Christ and Cyrus
english: You hear how he says, 'You do not know me,' and he does not consider himself worthy to be ranked with the renowned God, who is the master of many nations and greater than kings, for the things accomplished through Christ were types.
He foretold the destruction of Babylon's false prophecies and the signs of the ventriloquists, as well as the plans of his own prophets, which were not false.

He also foretold that he would rebuild the cities of Judah and desolate the abyss, which refers to Babylon due to the large number of inhabitants, and dry up all its rivers, which refer to the nations flowing in from all sides to provide assistance.

Cyrus was the son of Mandane, the daughter of Astyages, the ruler of the Medes, and the father of Cambyses, a Persian by birth; and some of the ancients called him half-mule and of mixed nature, which can also be seen in Christ, who was born of the holy Virgin and had no human father, but was of a different nature, surpassing all created things.
He spoke to the Jews, who thought they were with us and that it happened with us, saying, 'You are from below, while I am from above' (John 8:23).

This contrast is reminiscent of the difference between the earthly kingdom of Cyrus, who ruled over many nations and was received by every city, and the heavenly kingdom of Emmanuel, who rules under heaven and is received by every city as Savior and Redeemer.
The latter has freed humanity from slavery and devilish greed, and has even gone down to Hades, emptying dark, secret, and invisible treasures, and through him Israel was given to long slavery.
He broke bronze doors and iron bars, saying to those in bonds, 'Come out' (Isaiah 61:1), and to those in darkness, 'Be revealed' (Isaiah 61:1).

He also said to Job, the most patient and undefeated athlete, 'You came to the spring of the sea and walked in the footsteps of the abyss' (Job 38:16), and the gates of death opened to him, and the gatekeepers of Hades fled in fear.
…demonstrating the…
translator_notes: The text begins and ends mid-sentence; '...demonstrating the...' renders the fragment 'καταδεικνύντος το'.
The phrase 'ἀποκρύ φους' is a fragmented rendering of 'ἀποκρύφους' (secret/hidden).
The phrase 'πατρὸς δὲ Καμβύσου' identifies Cambyses as the son of the previously mentioned father.
The translation of 'ἑτεροφυᾶ' as 'of mixed nature' is based on the context describing the hybrid nature of Cyrus.

title: Melchizedek's Significance
english: God speaks to his people through their brothers, just as he speaks to us, and he gives his words to them to proclaim to others as he commands.
We see this in the example of Jesus, the son of Nave, who led the Israelites across the Jordan and into the promised land, circumcising them with flint knives along the way.
In the same way, we have been baptized and circumcised in Christ, receiving a spiritual circumcision that makes us heirs of the kingdom of heaven.
This is not a mysterious or obscure concept, but rather one that is clearly demonstrated in the scriptures.
For instance, the Spirit is not limited to a particular form or image, but rather is present in each of the saints, honoring the Son and demonstrating the truth of God's word.
The idea that Melchizedek was a divine being, rather than a human one, is a foolish notion that is contradicted by the scriptures.
The fact that he blessed Abraham, who was greater than he, demonstrates that the lesser is blessed by the greater.
The scriptures tell us that Melchizedek was without father, without mother, and without genealogy, and yet he blessed Abraham.
As it is written, 'The lesser is blessed by the greater' (Hebrews 7:7).
I have been utterly astonished by the manner in which some people approach the figure of Abraham.
It seems to me that they have lost sight of the true nature of his significance, and instead have become mired in a futile pursuit of knowledge.

For they attempt to understand Melchizedek, who is presented as a likeness and type of Emmanuel, by examining the external trappings of his priesthood, rather than seeking to comprehend the deeper truths that he represents.
In doing so, they torment themselves with unnecessary and unproductive speculations.
The question that arises, then, is what is the source of their confusion.
Why do they insist on seeking to understand the nature of Melchizedek's priesthood, when it is clear that the true significance of his blessing of Abraham lies elsewhere?
Is it not because they are failing to distinguish between the shadows and the reality, and are instead becoming entangled in the enigmas of the former?
For it is only by looking beyond the external signs and symbols to the deeper truths that they represent that we can hope to gain a true understanding.
Aaron was blameless, having been appointed and being the leader of the holy tabernacle, crowned with the highest honors in priesthood.
How then was he sanctified?
translator_notes: The Greek text may be fragmented or incomplete in some places, but I have translated it as literally as possible, indicating where the text appears to be cut off with an ellipsis (...).
I have omitted untranslatable partial letters at the edges of the text and noted each edge cut in the translator's notes.
The translation attempts to preserve the original word order and meaning, while still conveying the author's intended message in natural literary prose.
